Higher loads are more advantageous for maximal strength, while lower loads can still stimulate hypertrophy when the training stimulus is adequate. Therefore the coach should not claim that one narrow repetition range is the only effective range for muscle growth.

chunks.evidence_text: Meta-analytic evidence does not show that taking every resistance-training set to momentary muscular failure is necessary for hypertrophy. A 2023 systematic review found no clear superiority of momentary failure over non-failure training, while a 2024 meta-regression found that hypertrophy tended to increase as sets were terminated closer to failure. These findings support effortful training without making momentary failure a universal requirement.

source.title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis

chunks.evidence_text: A 2024 Bayesian systematic review found substantial overlap among different inter-set rest durations. The evidence suggested a small hypertrophy benefit to resting longer than 60 seconds, possibly because longer rests help preserve training volume, while differences above roughly 90 seconds were not appreciable in that analysis. Rest should therefore be adjusted to maintain useful training quality rather than imposed as a rigid rule.

chunks.evidence_text: Progression is a core principle of resistance training: the training stimulus must remain sufficiently challenging as a person adapts. A 2026 randomized study reported greater muscle growth with progressive overload than without overload progression in the studied population, while noting that training without progression can still produce hypertrophy in some previously untrained people. The coach should therefore treat progression as a useful strategy, not as a promise that every session must increase load.
